content: Good morning. I have some significant news to share today, and honestly I have been looking forward to telling you. We have finally made a hire for the head chef position at Osteria Morishita. It took longer than I originally hoped — I would say close to six weeks from the time we first started reaching out to candidates until we actually had a signed contract in hand — but I am very confident that we found exactly the right person. The search was exhausting at moments, particularly in weeks three and four when I was starting to worry we might need to push the opening timeline back if we could not find someone who fit the concept. But we got there, and I think when I tell you the full story you will understand why I feel so settled about the decision.

Good morning, Kenta-san. That is genuinely exciting news — congratulations on closing that hire, and I can hear the relief in how you are describing it. Six weeks is a real investment of time and attention, especially when you are also managing the interior build-out, the branding transition from Ginza Trattoria to Osteria Morishita, and all the supplier relationships that need to be in place before you open. The fact that you held out rather than settling for someone who was almost right suggests you had a clear picture of what you needed, which is the first requirement for a search like this to succeed. I want to hear everything — who you hired, how the candidate pool looked across those six weeks, what the deciding factors were, and how the practical details of the contract came together. Please take it from the beginning.

His name is Marco Petrelli. He is 38 years old, which I think is actually an ideal age for this kind of role — experienced enough to command a kitchen, to have made his significant mistakes already and learned from them, but still young enough to have genuine energy and ambition rather than someone who is coasting. He is originally from Modena, which in the context of what we are building at Osteria Morishita is almost poetic. We have been very deliberate about anchoring our menu to the northern Italian regions, particularly Emilia-Romagna, Lombardy, Piemonte, and having a head chef who grew up in Modena means that sensibility is not studied or adopted — it is genuinely native to him. The pasta traditions, the slow-cooked meat dishes, the relationship with aged products, the way that cuisine thinks about fat and richness and texture — that is his mother tongue. His most recent position was at Ristorante Acqua Pazza, the Italian restaurant in Daikanyama that has a very good reputation for serious regional cooking without trying to be flashy about it. He spent 4 years there in total, the first three as sous chef and the final year as head chef when the previous head left to open his own place. We signed the contract last week and I am still a little stunned that it came together the way it did.

Marco Petrelli — I want to make sure I am tracking this correctly. Ristorante Acqua Pazza in Daikanyama is a house with a real identity, not a generic Italian operation. If I recall correctly, it has been regarded as one of the more thoughtful regional Italian kitchens in that part of Tokyo, with a wine list that takes the cuisine seriously rather than just serving what sells. Four years at a single restaurant, with an internal promotion to the top of the kitchen rather than needing to be recruited from outside — that is a meaningful signal. It tells you the people who worked alongside him most closely trusted him enough to hand him the keys when the moment came. The Modena origin is worth dwelling on for a moment because it shapes the palate in very specific ways. Emilia-Romagna is probably the most technically demanding of the northern Italian regional cuisines — the pasta work is intricate, the ragù requires patience and a particular understanding of how collagen and fat behave over long cooking times, the relationship with Parmigiano-Reggiano and aged aceto balsamico tradizionale is about restraint and timing rather than volume. A chef who grew up eating those things as home food, not as restaurant food, has a completely different reference point. Did his cooking during the trial cook actually reflect that regional depth, or did you find he had moved toward something more broadly contemporary in his style?

The trial cook was extraordinary, honestly. I set it up as a half-day event in the Osteria Morishita kitchen — we are still in the equipment-testing phase so not everything is fully calibrated, and I told him upfront that the environment would be imperfect, partly as a practical reality and partly because I wanted to see how he responded to constraints. He arrived forty minutes early, walked the kitchen slowly without saying much, asked the kitchen manager two very specific questions about the oven calibration and where the heavy copper pans were stored, and then he just began. For the trial cook he prepared three dishes. The first was a tagliatelle al ragù — classic, foundational, the kind of dish where you immediately know whether someone understands the cuisine at a structural level. He made the pasta by hand in front of the whole team, and his technique was exceptional in a way that was almost quiet. No showmanship, no commentary, just the kind of practiced confidence that comes from doing something ten thousand times. The sheet was thin without being fragile, the cut was consistent, and the ragù had clearly been developed over many hours, with a depth of flavor that you simply cannot rush. The second dish was a tortellini in brodo that he said his grandmother in Modena taught him when he was very young, and I will be completely honest with you — I nearly hired him on that dish alone. The broth was luminous and had been built from a proper mix of capon and beef with vegetables roasted to a specific shade, and the tortellini were the size of a thumb tip, the pasta thin enough to be almost translucent around the filling. It was the kind of dish that makes you feel like you are being trusted with something. The third dish was more deliberately contemporary, a roasted duck breast with a Lambrusco reduction and shaved truffle, which demonstrated that he can move beyond the canon when the context calls for it without losing the disciplined sensibility underneath. What struck me as much as the food itself was the way the kitchen staff watched him the entire time. Nobody drifted, nobody checked their phones, nobody had a side conversation. They were genuinely engaged and I think a little in awe. That told me as much about his presence as the food did.

The tortellini in brodo detail is the one I would weight most heavily out of everything you just described. That dish is almost a trap for chefs who have technique without genuine depth, because there is nowhere to hide. The broth has to be impeccably clear, properly seasoned, and built from real stock work over many hours — you cannot reduce or concentrate your way to the right result quickly. The filling inside a tortellini is compressed into a very small space, which means every component of it has to carry its own weight. The pasta itself has to be thin enough to feel delicate in the mouth but structurally sound enough to hold the filling through the cooking process. Any serious cook can learn the mechanics of assembling tortellini, but cooking them at the level you are describing — the kind of dish that makes you feel like you are being trusted with something, as you put it — requires that the person making it grew up eating the right version and has that reference point built into their body rather than learned from a recipe book. The fact that he attributed it to his grandmother in Modena rather than to a mentor chef or a culinary training program tells you something important: this is family knowledge, and people who cook from family knowledge have a completely different emotional relationship with the dish than people who cook from a plated photograph in a culinary textbook. As for the kitchen team staying engaged for the full trial — you are right that this is a significant signal. Line cooks are a brutally honest audience. They are tired, they are skeptical of outsiders, and they have no professional obligation to pretend to be interested. If they were watching, it was because he was doing something worth watching. How did the broader search unfold before Marco entered the picture? You mentioned six weeks — what did the earlier phases look like?

The early phase was honestly discouraging. We used a culinary recruitment agency for the first round, and we interviewed four candidates through them over the first three weeks. Not a single one of them was quite right, and interestingly the reasons were all different, which made it difficult to simply redefine the brief and try again. The first two candidates were technically strong — you could see that immediately — but both of them had spent the majority of their careers in Japanese-Italian fusion contexts, the kind of restaurant that uses Italian structure as a loose framework and then layers in Japanese ingredients and Japanese sensibility in ways that blur the regional character. That is a legitimate genre and there are places in Tokyo doing it beautifully, but it is not what Osteria Morishita is. We are a northern Italian restaurant, specifically and deliberately, and I did not want to hire someone whose primary creative instinct would be to reframe everything through a Japanese lens. The third candidate had a genuinely impressive CV — some years in Italy, some serious Tokyo restaurants — but when we sat in the interview I could feel something was missing. He talked about cooking in a way that had become transactional. He talked about hours as a burden, about the demands of the craft as something that had worn him down. He was a burned-out version of someone who had probably been excellent five years ago, and no salary or title was going to fix that. The fourth was probably the most painful because he had real promise — he was twenty-nine, he had done a stage in Turin and worked at two good restaurants in Tokyo — but he was genuinely not ready to head a kitchen. You could see the instincts forming, but they were not yet automatic in the way they need to be when you are responsible for the entire output of a kitchen every service. I sent his information to a colleague who runs a smaller operation and suggested they stay in touch with him in a year or two. Then came the referral that changed everything. Our wine supplier, Mariko Nakata from Nakata Shoji, mentioned she had a contact through the import trade community who might be exactly what we were looking for. Mariko has been working restaurant accounts across Tokyo for many years and she has a genuinely remarkable network in the industry. She introduced us to Marco Petrelli through those industry contacts, and from the very first phone call it was obvious we were speaking to a completely different caliber of candidate.

The way you have described those four early candidates maps almost perfectly to the four failure modes of chef hiring: technically capable but wrong concept fit, technically capable but wrong culinary DNA, technically capable but emotionally depleted, and genuinely talented but not yet ready for the scope of the role. Those are four distinct problems and you handled each of them correctly by not trying to bend the role to fit the candidate. The instinct to forward the fourth candidate's information to a colleague rather than just file it away is worth noting — that kind of practical generosity tends to come back in useful ways in a small industry. Now, the Mariko Nakata referral is interesting to me on multiple levels. A wine supplier representative who covers restaurant accounts across Tokyo is, in a certain sense, better positioned to know the actual state of the chef talent market than any formal recruiter. Formal recruiters see candidates who are actively looking and have chosen to engage with a process. Mariko is in the kitchen at delivery time, she is at the pass when things are calm, she sits through end-of-service conversations when people are honest and a little tired. She knows who the serious people are, who is quietly thinking about a change, who is frustrated with their current situation, and critically, who would be a meaningful fit for a particular concept because she understands the concepts intimately through the lens of building wine programs for them. A referral that arrives through industry contacts of that kind comes pre-filtered in a way that a CV submission through an agency cannot replicate. It also carries a layer of mutual accountability — Marco knows that Mariko's professional standing is in some sense attached to this introduction, which adds weight to his own seriousness about it. How did the Nakata-san conversation actually happen? Did she proactively come to you, or did it emerge from something you said?

It was almost accidental in the way that the most important things often are. Mariko was in for our monthly wine tasting — we had a long afternoon session working through the opening cellar list, going bottle by bottle through the Piemonte and Emilia-Romagna selections, deciding what would anchor the list and what would fill in around it. It was a good session but I was clearly distracted, and at some point I said something offhand about the agency candidates being a disappointment, that I was worried we might not have the right head chef in place before we needed to. She did not react visibly at the time, she did not make a promise or suggest she had anyone in mind, and we moved on and finished the tasting. But about three days later she called me directly — not through email, she actually phoned — and she said she had thought about what I mentioned and that she had spoken to someone she felt might be exactly what I had described. That was Marco Petrelli. She had seen him during a routine delivery visit to Ristorante Acqua Pazza a few weeks earlier, and he had told her during their conversation that after 4 years there he was starting to think seriously about his next step. He said he felt ready for something that would be his own project to build rather than executing someone else's established vision. She remembered that when I mentioned the search, and she made the connection. The timing was almost uncanny. I have already told her that she is getting a reservation on opening night and the best table in the room, and she laughed and said she would take it only if Marco's cooking is as good as she told me it would be. Now of course I also owe her a very good dinner once we are fully running.

The detail that Mariko called rather than emailed is small but meaningful — it signals that she was treating this as a personal matter, a careful introduction rather than a casual forwarding of contact information. People reach for the phone when they want to be present in the conversation rather than simply transmitting a message. She clearly thought about it deliberately over those three days and decided she was willing to put her own name behind this introduction in a way that carries real weight in a close-knit industry. The thing Marco said about wanting something that felt like his own project rather than someone else's established vision is worth sitting with carefully, because it is simultaneously the most compelling thing about him and the thing that will require the most thoughtful management going forward. A chef who has spent 4 years executing a kitchen's inherited identity and is hungry to build something original will bring an extraordinary level of energy, creative investment, and genuine ownership to Osteria Morishita. He will arrive early to solve problems you have not yet identified. He will think about the menu during his days off. He will care about the restaurant in the way that an employee who is merely well-compensated never quite does. All of that is enormously valuable to you. At the same time, Osteria Morishita is your concept, your address at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, your name on the door in the form of the restaurant brand you are building, your vision of what northern Italian cooking should feel like in this particular neighborhood. The key is to establish early — ideally before the first service, while everyone is still in the constructive phase — a shared language about where Marco has full creative authority over the menu, the kitchen culture, the cooking processes, and where decisions come back to you as the owner. That clarity, established when relationships are healthy and forward-looking, prevents an enormous amount of friction later when the restaurant is under pressure and both of you are tired. How did the contract negotiations go? I imagine getting the structure right there was important.

The contract negotiations were actually smoother than I expected, and I think that is in part because Marco came to them with a clear and reasonable sense of his own market value rather than either underselling himself or opening at a number designed to test my reaction. We spent most of two conversations on the structure. We agreed on a monthly salary of 720,000 yen, which I will be honest is toward the higher end of what I had originally budgeted for this role, but when I sat down and thought about it seriously it is absolutely appropriate compensation for someone of his experience profile — eight years of serious Italian restaurant work, four of them in Tokyo, with the last year running a full kitchen. I would rather pay correctly and have someone who feels respected from day one than save sixty thousand yen a month and have someone who feels undervalued. Beyond the base, we also structured a 13-month bonus structure tied to quarterly performance reviews, and that was actually Marco's suggestion, not mine. He came into the second negotiation conversation with the idea already formed: he wanted a meaningful portion of his compensation to have some connection to how the restaurant actually performs rather than everything being guaranteed regardless of outcome. We agreed on criteria that include kitchen cost management, guest feedback scores, and whether we hit the revenue targets for each quarter. I found that instinct to be a genuinely healthy sign — it means he sees himself as accountable for the restaurant's success rather than just for the quality of the food that leaves his kitchen, which is exactly the kind of integrated thinking I need in a head chef. As for timing, the start date is September 1, 2025, which I am very happy about. That puts him in the restaurant two full weeks before our planned soft opening, which means he will be with us from the beginning of the final kitchen build-out, the last equipment decisions, the menu finalization, all of it.

A monthly salary of 720,000 yen with a 13-month bonus structure is a well-constructed package, and I want to reflect back why each element of it is right for what you are building. The base is honest — you described it as toward the higher end of your budget, but paying at market or slightly above market for a critical hire is almost always the correct financial decision when you account for the cost of getting this wrong. A head chef search that fails and needs to be restarted costs you six weeks of time, agency fees, a delay in opening, and the reputational cost of going to market twice, which signals to the candidate pool that there is something unresolved about the concept or the operator. The 13-month bonus structure is the more interesting element, and Marco's instinct to propose it rather than simply negotiating a higher base tells you something important about how he thinks about the relationship between his work and the restaurant's viability. A chef who wants his compensation tied to quarterly performance reviews has made a decision to understand the business, not just the kitchen. He will pay attention to food cost percentages in a way that someone on a flat guaranteed salary might not. He will think about the relationship between menu engineering and margin. He will have a stake in whether the quarterly revenue targets are met, which means he will have a stake in the guest experience in a holistic way — not just whether the food is excellent, but whether the whole visit results in the kind of satisfaction that brings people back. The September 1, 2025 start date is exceptionally well-timed and I want to underscore why. Having Marco in the building two weeks before the soft opening means the menu you open with is genuinely his menu, shaped by his hands and his palate and his creative decisions from the beginning, not a specification handed to him by someone else that he is executing without full authorship. He will be present for the equipment calibration conversations, the final supplier meetings — including the ongoing wine program work with Mariko Nakata at Nakata Shoji, which is a relationship that now has an additional layer of meaning given how the introduction happened. He will establish his own rhythms with the kitchen team before the pressure of actual service begins. He will solve problems in the space that nobody has anticipated yet, which always happens in a new kitchen regardless of how carefully everything has been planned. A few things worth doing in these two weeks before he starts: formalize in writing the creative authority boundaries I mentioned, not as constraints on Marco but as a shared reference point so you both have the same understanding of the decision-making structure. Schedule a working session with Marco and Mariko Nakata together before the opening — she introduced them, she will be a frequent presence at the restaurant as the wine supplier, and getting those three professional relationships into the same room early creates a foundation of mutual context that will serve everyone well. And document in detail the performance metrics that will drive the 13-month bonus structure now, while all three parties are aligned and optimistic, rather than trying to construct shared definitions of success mid-year when there may be tension about what the numbers actually mean. What you have assembled here — the concept, the location at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, the wine relationship with Nakata Shoji, and now Marco Petrelli as the head chef who brings genuine Modena roots and eight years of serious craft — is a cohesive and credible foundation. You should feel good about where this stands.
